subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of these best illustrates that the universe is unimaginably vast in scale?
options: The Milky Way is the only galaxy
All stars are within one light-year of Earth
There are estimated to be billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars
The Sun is the only star in the universe
questions.explain: The observable universe contains billions of galaxies, each holding billions of stars, showing its enormous scale.

questions.q: Astronomers infer the existence of dark matter mainly because galaxies:
options: Are too bright to be ordinary stars
Rotate faster than their visible mass alone can explain
questions.explain: The outer parts of galaxies rotate faster than the visible matter can account for, implying extra unseen 'dark' matter.

questions.q: A redshift in a galaxy's spectrum means its light has been stretched towards which end of the visible spectrum?
options: It is not shifted at all
questions.explain: Recession stretches light to longer wavelengths, shifting spectral lines towards the red end of the spectrum.

questions.q: The Sun is located:
options: At the edge of the universe
At the exact centre of the Milky Way
In one of the spiral arms, far from the centre
questions.explain: The Sun sits in a minor spiral arm roughly halfway out from the galaxy's centre, about 26,000 light-years from the core.

questions.q: Elliptical galaxies differ from spiral galaxies in that they:
options: Are rounded or oval with little gas and few new stars
questions.explain: Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars with little star formation.

questions.q: A planet that orbits a star other than the Sun is called a/an:
questions.explain: Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars beyond our own solar system.

questions.q: The faint band of light crossing the night sky that gives our galaxy its name is caused by:
options: The combined light of countless distant stars in the galactic disc
questions.explain: Looking along the plane of our own galaxy, we see the merged light of vast numbers of stars as the Milky Way band.

questions.q: The discovery of the cosmic microwave background radiation in the 1960s supported the Big Bang because it matched:
options: The predicted faint, cooled afterglow filling the whole sky
questions.explain: The Big Bang predicted leftover radiation, now cooled to microwaves, evenly filling the sky, which is exactly what was found.

questions.q: Which of these is the largest in scale?
questions.explain: A galaxy contains billions of stars and their systems, far larger than a single solar system.

questions.q: In the formation of a planetary system, the planets form from material in the:
options: Protoplanetary disc of gas and dust around the young star
questions.explain: Planets grow by accretion of dust and gas within the flat protoplanetary disc orbiting the new star.

questions.q: One parsec is approximately equal to:
questions.explain: A parsec is about 3.26 light-years, the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of one arcsecond.

questions.q: A galaxy with no clear shape or spiral structure is classified as:
questions.explain: Irregular galaxies lack the ordered spiral or elliptical form.

questions.q: Dark energy is the name given to whatever is causing the expansion of the universe to:
questions.explain: Observations show the universe's expansion is speeding up, and this acceleration is attributed to dark energy.

questions.q: One common method of detecting exoplanets is the transit method, which looks for:
options: A small regular dip in a star's brightness as a planet passes in front of it
Changes in the star's colour over millions of years
questions.explain: When a planet transits its star, it blocks a tiny fraction of the starlight, causing a small periodic dip in brightness.

questions.q: The nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way, on a collision course with us in the far future, is:
questions.explain: The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest large spiral galaxy and is approaching the Milky Way.

questions.q: The Big Bang theory states that the universe:
options: Began from a hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since
Was created by a collision of two galaxies
questions.explain: The Big Bang describes the universe expanding and cooling from an extremely hot, dense beginning.

questions.q: Hubble found that more distant galaxies are generally:
questions.explain: Hubble's law states recession speed is proportional to distance, supporting an expanding universe.

questions.q: The constant in Hubble's law (the Hubble constant) relates a galaxy's recession speed to its:
questions.explain: Hubble's law states recession velocity equals the Hubble constant multiplied by distance, so the constant links speed to distance.

questions.q: The Milky Way is broadly classified as what type of galaxy?
questions.explain: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy with arms winding out from a central bulge.

questions.q: Roughly how many stars does a typical large galaxy like the Milky Way contain?
questions.explain: The Milky Way contains on the order of a few hundred billion stars.

questions.q: The cosmic microwave background radiation is important because it is:
options: Leftover radiation that is strong evidence for the Big Bang
questions.explain: The CMB is faint radiation from the early universe, a key piece of evidence for the Big Bang.

questions.q: The redshift of light from distant galaxies is evidence that the universe is:
questions.explain: Light from distant galaxies is stretched to longer (redder) wavelengths, showing space is expanding.
